notes.meaning: Moses gathered all Israel in the desert plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River, to speak God's words to them. Because the crowd was so huge, he spoke to the elders and leaders, who then shared his message with everyone else. Naming these desert places reminded the people of where they had journeyed and how God kept them safe despite their past sins.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars believe the phrase 'east of the Jordan' shows that Deuteronomy was composed later by writers already living inside the land of Canaan, rather than written by Moses on the plains of Moab.

notes.meaning: A normal walk from Mount Horeb to Kadesh-barnea takes only eleven days. Moses pointed this out to remind Israel that taking forty years to reach the border was not caused by distance. Their long delay happened entirely because their fathers rebelled against God.

On the first day of the eleventh month in the fortieth year after leaving Egypt, Moses repeated God's commands to the Israelites. With only weeks left before his death, he faithfully shared everything the Lord told him. He made sure this new generation knew God's law before they stepped into their new homeland.

Before this speech, God gave Israel victory over Sihon and Og, two powerful Amorite kings. Winning those battles showed the people that God's power was active and reliable. These triumphs gave the new generation great confidence to trust the Lord for the rest of Canaan.

East of the Jordan River in the land of Moab, Moses willingly began to explain God's law clearly. The older generation had passed away in the desert, so the younger people needed to hear the covenant explained for their own lives. Moses taught them carefully so they would know how to obey God in the promised land.

Moses reminded the people of the time God spoke to them at Mount Horeb, which is Mount Sinai. The Lord told them they had stayed at that mountain long enough. They had spent nearly a whole year learning God's laws, and it was now time to get up and go.

The Lord ordered Israel to break camp and march toward the hill country of the Amorites and all neighboring regions. He outlined the full territory He planned to give them, stretching from the southern desert to the Mediterranean Sea and all the way to the Euphrates River. God set broad borders before them to encourage them on their journey.

God told the Israelites that He had placed the land right in front of them to possess. Taking the land was not an invasion of someone else's property, but receiving a gift from the Lord. God had promised this land by a solemn oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and now He was ready to give it to their children.

Moses reminded the people that back at Sinai, he admitted he could not lead them all by himself. Guiding and managing such a huge group was far too heavy for any single person. He humbly recognized his own limits and asked for help rather than trying to rule alone.

The Lord had multiplied Israel so greatly that they had become as numerous as the stars in the night sky. This amazing growth showed that God had kept the covenant promise He made to Abraham centuries before. Even during harsh years of slavery, God had preserved and expanded His people.

Moses prayed that the Lord would multiply the people a thousand times more and pour out every blessing He had promised. Even though leading such a large nation was demanding, Moses truly celebrated their growth. His heart desired to see God's promises overflow in their lives.

Moses asked how he could possibly handle all the people's troubles, daily burdens, and personal arguments on his own. In a huge community, many disputes arise that require careful listening and wise decisions. Moses needed a dependable system of justice to keep peace among the tribes.

Moses told the tribes to choose men known for wisdom, good judgment, and respect. He did not force his own favorites upon them, but let the people pick capable leaders from their own families. Once the tribes selected these godly men, Moses appointed them to serve as judges.

The Israelites agreed with Moses and told him that his proposal was good. They welcomed the plan to share the work of government among trusted men from every tribe. Because the people consented to this arrangement, they had a duty to respect the judges they helped choose.

Moses took the wise and respected leaders chosen by the tribes and gave them authority over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. He also named officers to assist them in running tribal matters. This organized network made sure that everyone had access to fair leadership and prompt help.

Moses gave strict orders to the new judges to hear every dispute fairly. They were commanded to listen to both sides before making a decision. They also had to treat native Israelites and foreign visitors with the exact same standard of justice.

Judges were commanded never to show favoritism or be frightened by powerful people, because true judgment belongs to God. A judge acts as God's representative and must reflect His honesty and fairness. Any case that was too hard or complicated for the local judges was to be brought directly to Moses.

At that same time, Moses gave the people and their judges all the instructions and duties they needed to follow. God gave them a complete standard of life so they could live in peace and righteousness. Knowing God's rules prepared the whole nation for the march ahead.

Following God's command, Israel left Mount Horeb and traveled through the vast and frightening desert. That dry, rocky wilderness was dangerous, but God's presence guided them safely through it until they arrived at Kadesh-barnea. Remembering how God protected them along that hard road gave them every reason to trust Him.

When they arrived at Kadesh-barnea, Moses announced that they had reached the hill country of the Amorites. He told them that the Lord was now handing this land over to them. They were standing right at the doorway to their new home.

Moses told the Israelites that God had placed the land right before them, so they should go up and take it immediately. He urged them not to be afraid or lose heart, because the Lord had already promised them victory. All they had to do was step forward in bold faith.

Instead of moving forward in faith, the people came to Moses and suggested sending spies first to check out the roads and cities. While this seemed like practical planning, it revealed that they doubted God's word and wanted to rely on human sight. God had already promised the land was good, but they still wanted proof.

The idea of sending spies seemed reasonable to Moses, so he chose twelve men, one leader from each tribe. Moses agreed to the request in good faith, and God permitted the mission to test their hearts. Looking back, Moses remembered how this plan quickly opened the door to fear and rebellion.
